name: Phyllanthaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use the project's Phyllanthus architecture to teach the modern split from Euphorbiaceae: no latex, two ovules per locule, no conspicuous seed caruncle, plus phyllanthoid branching.

project_scope.note: The family was historically embedded in broad Euphorbiaceae. The learner should make the modern split explicit rather than teaching all leafflowers as spurges.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: On local Phyllanthus, inspect the branching first: flattened or horizontal leafy branchlets can mimic a compound leaf, with small simple leaves arranged in two ranks. Then confirm tiny unisexual flowers, no milky latex and a usually 3-lobed schizocarp/capsule.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Local project plants are herbs/subshrubs with simple entire stipulate leaves. Phyllanthoid branching may create upright main axes with reduced cataphylls and lateral deciduous leafy/floriferous branchlets.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are unisexual and small, commonly with sepals but no petals. Ovary superior and commonly 3-carpellate/3-locular, with two ovules per locule.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a 3-lobed dehiscent schizocarp/capsule around a persistent central columella; seeds lack the conspicuous caruncle typical of many Euphorbiaceae.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Compound-leaf lookalike branchlets + tiny unisexual apetalous flowers + no latex + 3-lobed fruit is the local Phyllanthus pattern.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: phyllanthoid branchlet → tiny unisexual flowers → 2 ovules/locule → 3-lobed fruit/columella → Euphorbiaceae split → native-vs-introduced project species
visual_lesson.intro: Leafflowers are perfect for learning why modern taxonomy split Phyllanthaceae from Euphorbiaceae. They share a three-part fruit plan, but the ovules and latex tell a different story.

steps.title: 1 · Decide whether that 'compound leaf' is really a branch
steps.look_for: Small simple leaves arranged distichously on a lateral branchlet; flowers/fruits arise from its leaf axils.
steps.why_it_matters: Phyllanthoid branching is one of the most useful genus-level visual cues.

steps.title: 2 · Find the tiny male and female flowers
steps.look_for: Tiny unisexual flowers, usually without petals, often tucked beneath the small leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects the genus to its broader Malpighiales reproductive architecture.

steps.title: 3 · Use the ovule count to split from Euphorbiaceae
steps.look_for: Typically two ovules in each locule rather than the one-ovule-per-locule pattern common in Euphorbiaceae.
steps.why_it_matters: This is one of the cleanest technical family separators in the project.

steps.title: 4 · Confirm the 3-lobed fruit and columella
steps.look_for: Three lobes/cocci separating from a central column as the fruit dehisces.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows why the family can look euphorb-like while still being distinct.

steps.title: 5 · Check latex—but only as supporting evidence
steps.look_for: Phyllanthaceae generally lacks the white latex common in many Euphorbiaceae.
steps.why_it_matters: Helpful paired with ovule count; not a reason to damage unknown plants unnecessarily.

comparisons.title: Phyllanthaceae vs Euphorbiaceae
comparisons.rule: Phyllanthaceae generally lacks latex, has two ovules per locule and seeds without a conspicuous caruncle; Euphorbiaceae often has latex, one ovule per locule and frequently carunculate seeds. Both may have a 3-part columella fruit.

comparisons.title: Phyllanthaceae vs Salicaceae
comparisons.rule: Phyllanthaceae usually has a multi-locular ovary with two ovules per locule; Salicaceae has a 1-locular ovary with parietal placentation, and local Salix/Populus makes many silky-haired seeds.

visual_lesson.caveat: Not every Phyllanthaceae species shows textbook phyllanthoid branching, but both project taxa are Phyllanthus, so it is a high-value local cue.

genera.fast_cue: distichous leaflike branchlets + tiny axillary unisexual flowers + 3-lobed fruit

taxonomy_notes: Phyllanthus polygonoides is accepted and native in Texas under current Kew.
Phyllanthus urinaria is accepted but introduced in Texas under current Kew; keep it as an introduced comparison rather than a native anchor.

visual_targets.annotation_goal: label main axis, lateral branchlet, individual leaves and axillary fruits
compare directly with Euphorbiaceae one-ovule pattern
